name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PHOTOSYNTHESISINHIGHERPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Contributions of early scientists in photosynthesis

questiontext.text:
Match the scientists in Column I with their key discoveries or experimental findings in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Joseph Priestley I. Demonstrated that sunlight is essential and oxygen bubbles form around green parts of aquatic plants
B. Jan Ingenhousz II. Deduced that oxygen evolved during green plant photosynthesis originates from water, not carbon dioxide
C. T.W. Engelmann III. Discovered oxygen and revealed that plants restore essential components to damaged air
D. Cornelius van Niel IV. Used a prism and Cladophora alga to plot the first action spectrum of photosynthesis

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the scientific contributions of each researcher
Joseph Priestley in 1770 performed bell-jar experiments showing that plants restore to air what burning candles and breathing animals remove, and later discovered oxygen in 1774.
Jan Ingenhousz showed that sunlight is indispensable for purifying fouled air and proved that green parts of aquatic plants release bubbles of oxygen in bright light.
T.W. Engelmann split light with a prism and illuminated Cladophora in an aerobic bacterial suspension, recording bacterial accumulation in blue and red zones to plot the first action spectrum.
Cornelius van Niel demonstrated through purple and green sulphur bacteria that photosynthesis is a light-dependent redox reaction and inferred that oxygen evolved by green plants comes from water rather than carbon dioxide.

Step 2: Match the paired entities
Joseph Priestley matches with discovery of oxygen and restoring damaged air.
Jan Ingenhousz matches with proving sunlight requirement and oxygen release by green parts.
T.W. Engelmann matches with prism-based action spectrum using Cladophora.
Cornelius van Niel matches with deducing that evolved oxygen originates from water.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with III, B with I, C with IV, and D with II.

questiontext.text:
Match the photosynthetic pigments listed in Column I with their corresponding colours observed on a chromatogram in Column II:

Column I (Pigment) Column II (Colour in chromatogram)
A. Chlorophyll a I. Yellow
B. Chlorophyll b II. Yellow to yellow-orange
C. Xanthophylls III. Bright or blue-green
D. Carotenoids IV. Yellow-green

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the chromatographic colour of each pigment
Paper chromatography separates four major pigments present in green leaves:
Chlorophyll a appears as bright or blue-green.
Chlorophyll b appears as yellow-green.
Xanthophylls show a distinct yellow band.
Carotenoids range in appearance from yellow to yellow-orange.

Step 2: Align the paired items
Chlorophyll a corresponds to bright or blue-green.
Chlorophyll b corresponds to yellow-green.
Xanthophylls correspond to yellow.
Carotenoids correspond to yellow to yellow-orange.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with III, B with IV, C with I, and D with II.

questiontext.text:
Match the structural compartments of the chloroplast in Column I with the specific photosynthetic events or features in Column II:

Column I (Structural Compartment) Column II (Photosynthetic Event / Feature)
A. Grana lamellae I. Enzymatic dark reactions leading to sugar synthesis
B. Stroma lamellae II. Water splitting and accumulation of protons in the lumen
C. Stroma matrix III. Houses both PS I and PS II for non-cyclic photophosphorylation
D. Inner side of thylakoid membrane IV. Performs cyclic photophosphorylation due to absence of PS II and NADP reductase

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the functional division of labour in the chloroplast
Grana thylakoid membranes contain both Photosystem I and Photosystem II and conduct non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
Stroma lamellae connect the grana, lack Photosystem II as well as NADP reductase enzyme, and run cyclic electron flow producing only ATP.
The stroma matrix contains soluble enzymes responsible for dark reactions (Calvin cycle) converting carbon dioxide to sugars.
The water-splitting complex is physically associated with Photosystem II on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane, releasing protons into the lumen.

Step 2: Determine the pairings
Grana lamellae match with containing both photosystems for non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
Stroma lamellae match with cyclic photophosphorylation due to lack of PS II and NADP reductase.
Stroma matrix matches with enzymatic reactions synthesizing sugar.
Inner side of thylakoid membrane matches with water splitting and proton accumulation in the lumen.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with III, B with IV, C with I, and D with II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PHOTOSYNTHESISINHIGHERPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Stages and energetics of the Calvin cycle

questiontext.text:
Match the stages and requirements of the Calvin cycle in Column I with their corresponding descriptions or quantities in Column II:

Column I (Calvin Cycle Stage / Metric) Column II (Description / Consumption)
A. Carboxylation I. Requires 1 molecule of ATP per \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) fixed to form the primary acceptor RuBP
B. Reduction II. Consumes 2 molecules of ATP and 2 molecules of NADPH per \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) fixed
C. Regeneration III. Involves fixation of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) onto RuBP catalysed by RuBisCO without ATP consumption
D. Synthesis of 1 hexose molecule IV. Requires 6 turns of the cycle consuming a total of 18 ATP and 12 NADPH

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate each stage of the Calvin cycle
Carboxylation is the addition of carbon dioxide to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate catalysed by RuBisCO to yield two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate; this specific step does not consume ATP or NADPH directly.
Reduction involves phosphorylation and reduction steps converting 3-PGA to triose phosphate, consuming 2 ATP and 2 NADPH per molecule of carbon dioxide.
Regeneration restores the carbon dioxide acceptor RuBP from triose phosphates and requires 1 ATP for phosphorylation.
To synthesize one 6-carbon glucose molecule, 6 turns of the cycle are needed, consuming \(6 \times 3 = 18\text{ ATP}\) and \(6 \times 2 = 12\text{ NADPH}\).

Step 2: Align the paired items
Carboxylation matches with fixation of carbon dioxide onto RuBP without ATP consumption.
Reduction matches with consumption of 2 ATP and 2 NADPH per carbon dioxide fixed.
Regeneration matches with requirement of 1 ATP per carbon dioxide to regenerate RuBP.
Synthesis of 1 hexose molecule matches with 6 turns consuming 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with III, B with II, C with I, and D with IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PHOTOSYNTHESISINHIGHERPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Comparative features of C3 and C4 pathways

questiontext.text:
Match the photosynthetic characteristics in Column I with their corresponding plant types or conditions in Column II:

Column I (Photosynthetic Characteristic) Column II (Plant Type / Pathway Feature)
A. Primary \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) acceptor is a 3-carbon molecule (PEP) I. \( \mathrm{C}_3 \) plants only
B. Calvin cycle takes place exclusively in bundle sheath cells II. \( \mathrm{C}_4 \) plants only
C. Photorespiration is absent or negligible due to high internal \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) III. Both \( \mathrm{C}_3 \) and \( \mathrm{C}_4 \) plants
D. Synthesis of sugars via the Calvin pathway IV. Characteristic of Kranz anatomy in \( \mathrm{C}_4 \) plants

Identify the correct matching for A, B, C, and D using the specific pairings below:

Column I Column II
A. Primary \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) acceptor is a 5-carbon ketose sugar (RuBP) I. Bundle sheath cells of \( \mathrm{C}_4 \) plants
B. Primary \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) acceptor is a 3-carbon compound (PEP) II. Mesophyll cells of \( \mathrm{C}_3 \) plants
C. Site of primary \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) fixation in \( \mathrm{C}_4 \) plants III. Mesophyll cells of \( \mathrm{C}_4 \) plants
D. Site of RuBisCO operation in \( \mathrm{C}_4 \) plants IV. Present in all photosynthetic plants

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the biochemistry of C3 and C4 photosynthetic pathways
In the C3 pathway, the primary carbon dioxide acceptor is ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP), a 5-carbon ketose sugar present in the mesophyll cells.
In the C4 pathway, the initial carbon dioxide acceptor is phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), a 3-carbon molecule found in the mesophyll cells.
Primary carbon dioxide fixation in C4 plants occurs in the mesophyll cells via PEP carboxylase.
RuBisCO is restricted to the bundle sheath cells in C4 plants, where decarboxylation of C4 acids releases carbon dioxide into the Calvin cycle.

Step 2: Match the entities directly
Primary carbon dioxide acceptor is a 5-carbon ketose sugar (RuBP) operates in mesophyll cells of C3 plants.
Primary carbon dioxide acceptor is a 3-carbon compound (PEP) functions in mesophyll cells of C4 plants.
Site of primary carbon dioxide fixation in C4 plants is the mesophyll cells.
Site of RuBisCO operation in C4 plants is the bundle sheath cells.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with II, B with III, C with III, and D with I. In standard one-to-one mapping across these options: RuBP corresponds to mesophyll cells of C3 plants, PEP corresponds to C4 mesophyll cells, primary carboxylation in C4 occurs in mesophyll cells, and RuBisCO operation in C4 takes place in bundle sheath cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PHOTOSYNTHESISINHIGHERPLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Mechanism of proton gradient development in chemiosmosis

questiontext.text:
Match the processes contributing to the chemiosmotic proton gradient in Column I with their direct physiological effect in Column II:

Column I (Process / Component) Column II (Effect on Proton Distribution)
A. Photolysis of water on the inner side of thylakoid membrane I. Removes protons directly from the stroma to form \( \mathrm{NADPH} + \mathrm{H}^+ \)
B. Primary electron acceptor transferring electrons to an H carrier II. Forms a transmembrane channel facilitating diffusion of protons from lumen to stroma
C. \( \mathrm{NADP} \) reductase enzyme on the stroma side III. Releases protons into the thylakoid lumen after picking them up from stroma
D. \( \mathrm{CF}_0 \) complex of ATP synthase IV. Accumulates protons directly inside the thylakoid lumen

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate each chemiosmotic component
Water photolysis occurs on the inner surface of the thylakoid membrane, causing direct release and accumulation of protons in the lumen.
The primary electron acceptor transfers electrons to a hydrogen carrier (plastoquinone), which removes protons from the stroma and unloads them into the inner lumen.
NADP reductase is situated on the stromal side of the membrane and consumes protons from the stroma along with electrons from PS I to produce NADPH.
The CF0 portion of ATP synthase is embedded across the membrane and acts as a channel for facilitated diffusion of protons down the concentration gradient from lumen back to stroma.

Step 2: Match the paired items
Photolysis of water matches with accumulation of protons directly inside the lumen.
Primary electron acceptor transferring to an H carrier matches with releasing protons into the lumen after taking them from stroma.
NADP reductase matches with removal of protons directly from the stroma.
CF0 complex matches with facilitating diffusion of protons from lumen to stroma.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with IV, B with III, C with I, and D with II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PHOTOSYNTHESISINHIGHERPLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Factors affecting photosynthesis and concentration thresholds

questiontext.text:
Match the environmental parameters and values in Column I with their corresponding photosynthetic significance in Column II:

Column I (Value / Parameter) Column II (Photosynthetic Significance)
A. 10 per cent of full sunlight I. Ambient atmospheric concentration of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \)
B. 0.03 to 0.04 per cent II. \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) saturation concentration for \( \mathrm{C}_4 \) plants
C. \( 360\,\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1} \) III. Light saturation point for most plants except shade or deep forest plants
D. Beyond \( 450\,\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1} \) IV. \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) saturation concentration for \( \mathrm{C}_3 \) plants

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Check facts and quantitative values from the NCERT text
Light saturation occurs at 10 percent of full sunlight, meaning light is rarely a limiting factor in open nature.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration currently lies between 0.03 and 0.04 percent (300 to 400 ppm).
C4 plants attain saturation at about \( 360\,\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1} \).
C3 plants respond to higher carbon dioxide levels and reach saturation only beyond \( 450\,\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1} \), which explains their enhanced yield in carbon dioxide enriched greenhouses.

Step 2: Align the paired items
10 percent of full sunlight corresponds to light saturation point for most plants.
0.03 to 0.04 percent corresponds to ambient atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide.
\( 360\,\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1} \) corresponds to carbon dioxide saturation for C4 plants.
Beyond \( 450\,\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1} \) corresponds to carbon dioxide saturation for C3 plants.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with III, B with I, C with II, and D with IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PHOTOSYNTHESISINHIGHERPLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Photosystems and electron transport chain components

questiontext.text:
Match the photosynthetic complexes/centres in Column I with their precise characteristics in Column II:

Column I (Photosystem / Carrier) Column II (Characteristic / Function)
A. Reaction centre of PS II I. Exhibits absorption peak at \( 700\,\mathrm{nm} \) and delivers excited electrons to an acceptor of high redox potential
B. Reaction centre of PS I II. Absorbs red light at \( 680\,\mathrm{nm} \) and is coupled to water splitting complex
C. Stroma lamellae membrane III. Cytochromes transferring electrons downhill on a redox potential scale without consuming them
D. Electron transport system (ETS) IV. Contains PS I only, lacks PS II and NADP reductase, supports cyclic photophosphorylation

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze each photochemical complex and carrier system
The reaction centre chlorophyll a of Photosystem II has an absorption maximum at \( 680\,\mathrm{nm} \) (called P680) and associates with the water-splitting complex on the thylakoid inner face.
The reaction centre chlorophyll a of Photosystem I has an absorption maximum at \( 700\,\mathrm{nm} \) (called P700) and passes electrons to an acceptor with high redox potential.
Stroma lamellae membranes lack both Photosystem II and NADP reductase enzyme, thus carrying out cyclic photophosphorylation involving only PS I.
The electron transport chain consisting of cytochromes mediates downhill electron transfer between the photosystems based on redox potential without consuming the electrons.

Step 2: Match the paired entities
Reaction centre of PS II matches with red light absorption at 680 nm and coupling to water splitting.
Reaction centre of PS I matches with absorption peak at 700 nm and transferring electrons to an acceptor of high redox potential.
Stroma lamellae membrane matches with containing PS I only, lacking PS II and NADP reductase.
Electron transport system matches with cytochromes transferring electrons downhill on a redox scale.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with II, B with I, C with IV, and D with III.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PHOTOSYNTHESISINHIGHERPLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Biochemical reactions of C4 pathway and photorespiration

questiontext.text:
Match the biochemical reactions/events in Column I with their appropriate descriptions or products in Column II:

Column I (Biochemical Event) Column II (Description / Resulting Products)
A. Oxygenase activity of RuBisCO in \( \mathrm{C}_3 \) plants I. Release of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) and a 3-carbon acid from a 4-carbon acid
B. Primary fixation step in mesophyll cells of \( \mathrm{C}_4 \) plants II. One molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate and one molecule of phosphoglycolate (2-carbon)
C. Decarboxylation in bundle sheath cells III. Catalysed by PEPcase yielding 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid (OAA)
D. Regeneration of PEP in mesophyll cells IV. Conversion of transported 3-carbon acid back to phosphoenolpyruvate

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the chemical reactions involved in C4 photosynthesis and photorespiration
When RuBisCO binds oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, RuBP is cleaved into one molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-carbon) and one molecule of 2-phosphoglycolate (2-carbon); this initiates the photorespiratory pathway.
In C4 mesophyll cells, PEPcase catalyses the carboxylation of 3-carbon PEP using bicarbonate, forming the 4-carbon acid oxaloacetate (OAA).
In bundle sheath cells, 4-carbon acids (malate or aspartate) undergo decarboxylation to release carbon dioxide into the Calvin cycle alongside a 3-carbon acid.
The 3-carbon acid returns to mesophyll cells where it is phosphorylated to regenerate the primary acceptor phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP).

Step 2: Match the paired entities
Oxygenase activity of RuBisCO matches with producing one molecule of 3-PGA and one molecule of phosphoglycolate.
Primary fixation step in C4 mesophyll cells matches with catalysed by PEPcase yielding OAA.
Decarboxylation in bundle sheath cells matches with release of carbon dioxide and a 3-carbon acid.
Regeneration of PEP matches with conversion of transported 3-carbon acid back to PEP.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with II, B with III, C with I, and D with IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PHOTOSYNTHESISINHIGHERPLANTS_MCQ_Q10 - Interpretation of light response curve regions

questiontext.text:
Refer to the standard curve depicting the rate of photosynthesis versus light intensity:

Match the regions/labels indicated on the graph in Column I with their correct physiological interpretations in Column II:

Column I (Graph Region / Point) Column II (Physiological Interpretation)
A. Region A I. Light intensity at which light saturation is attained (10% of full sunlight)
B. Region C II. Maximum rate of photosynthesis achieved where rate becomes constant
C. Point D III. Linear range where light is the direct limiting factor
D. Level E IV. Plateau region where light intensity is no longer limiting and other factors limit the rate

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the graph of light intensity versus photosynthetic rate
Region A represents low light intensities where there is a direct, linear relationship between light intensity and the rate of carbon dioxide fixation; here, light functions as the limiting factor.
Region C represents the plateau region at higher light intensities where the photosynthetic rate no longer increases with further increments of light; other factors like carbon dioxide concentration or temperature have become limiting.
Point D on the horizontal axis indicates the light intensity at which light saturation is reached (which corresponds to approximately 10 percent of full sunlight).
Level E on the vertical axis represents the maximum constant rate of photosynthesis achieved by the plant under these conditions.

Step 2: Match the paired entities
Region A corresponds to the linear range where light is the direct limiting factor.
Region C corresponds to the plateau region where light is no longer limiting and other factors limit the rate.
Point D corresponds to the light intensity at which saturation is reached.
Level E corresponds to the maximum rate of photosynthesis achieved.

Step 3: State the final conclusion
The correct matching sequence pairs A with III, B with IV, C with I, and D with II.
